briefings.title: BlackRock's Tony Kim on AI's Next Winners? Chips, Memory, Robotics & Quantum

people.name: Tony Kim
people.role: Managing Director and Head of Global Technology Team, BlackRock

briefings.tldr: Tony Kim, Managing Director and Head of the Global Technology Team within Fundamental Equities at BlackRock, breaks down how the AI boom is triggering a massive $1 trillion to $10 trillion compute-centric infrastructure rebuild, shifting focus from a software-dominated world to the physical layers of compute, power density, and memory.
briefings.summary_markdown:
## TL;DR
Tony Kim, Managing Director and Head of the Global Technology Team within Fundamental Equities at BlackRock, breaks down how the AI boom is triggering a massive $1 trillion to $10 trillion compute-centric infrastructure rebuild, shifting focus from a software-dominated world to the physical layers of compute, power density, and memory.

## Macro Value Transformation & The Compute Shift
* **Market Capitalization Inversion:**
  * **Software, Services, & Internet:** Roughly $10 trillion+ market cap (dominated pre-AI).
  * **Mag 7:** Roughly $22–$23 trillion market cap.
  * **Non-Mag 7 Chips & Hardware:** Roughly $30 trillion+ market cap, highlighting a deeply compute-hardware-centric market structure post-AI.
* **The Cloud Rebuild:** Pre-AI cloud infrastructure relied on commodity CPUs and hard drives running at megawatts; AI requires an "alien data center" architecture running at gigawatts and packing massive HBM/DRAM into servers costing millions instead of thousands of dollars.
* **Capital Expenditure Scale:** Roughly $1 trillion is being spent on CapEx this year, with $10 trillion expected over the next 5 years—ironically driven by the physical necessity to move data across increasingly shorter distances (from kilometers to meters, centimeters, and millimeters).

## Data Center Redesign, Physics, & The Power Grid
* **Physical Limits & Distance Reduction:** As compute density increases to pack more bits into smaller footprints, bandwidth, power, and heat scale logarithmically, forcing data center designs to their absolute physical limits.
* **Transition to Light:** Data center architectures are shifting from a regime of copper to a regime of light to handle power density and physical constraints.
* **Energy Infrastructure Re-engineering:** 
  * The power grid is undergoing a massive revolution driven by behind-the-meter generation and new nuclear Small Modular Reactors (SMRs).
  * New power architectures are emerging, led by the rise of 800-volt power systems and solid-state transformers to minimize energy loss during voltage step-downs.

## The RAMpocalypse & Co-Design Architecture
* **Skyrocketing Memory Intensity:** AI models and agentic harnesses are beginning to mirror the human brain, which is heavily memory-intensive compared to early compute-heavy AI architectures.
* **Memory & Compute Integration:** Chip architectures increasingly rely on tightly packed memory systems—including SRAM, DRAM, stacked DRAM, HBM, and high-bandwidth flash—co-designed directly with compute units.
* **Duration Mismatch:** A severe 3-to-4-year duration mismatch exists between current AI demand and the time required to build out new memory and chip fab capacities.

## Robotics, China, & Physical Embodiment
* **The Robotics Landscape:** Robotics architectures require a dual-brain system (an LLM for translation/communication and a world model for motor functions, motion, and perception) combined with a physical manufacturing body.
* **Global Robotics Disparity:** 
  * **China:** Driven by limited private market depth, China is aggressively using public markets as a funding mechanism, with 130 to 140 robotics companies and 30 to 40 potential IPOs projected this year.
  * **United States:** Only 1 to 2 robotics IPOs are expected in the U.S. this year.
* **Cross-Border Permutations:** A potential future market trend involves pairing advanced Western robotic brains with physical manufacturing bodies from Asian complexes in China, Korea, and Japan.
* **Social & Companion Robotics:** Beyond industrial use, massive demographic cliffs (such as birth rates below 1.0 in Asia and aging populations) will drive major markets for social, educational, and elderly companionship robots.

## Enterprise Workflows, Token Flow, & PE Roll-ups
* **Token Flow Dynamics:** Enterprise tech stacks are shifting toward an "ontology" or context layer sitting atop proprietary data foundations, orchestrating agents that interact via intelligence tokens. Companies must insert themselves into this token flow to capture value.
* **Private Equity & Operational Restructuring:** PE firms and venture funds are deploying roll-up strategies to buy traditional industries with massive cost inefficiencies, replacing legacy workflows with AI-driven stacks that generate equivalent revenue with a fraction of the headcount.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **Tony Kim:** Quantum computing utility scale, logically error-corrected million-qubit quantum computers will arrive by **2030**.
* **Tony Kim:** Regulatory approval and scaling of Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) and fusion will reach viability by **2030**.
* **Tony Kim:** Implementation of 800-volt power architectures and solid-state transformers in data centers will scale heavily by **2030**.
* **Tony Kim:** Orbital data centers will begin to truly scale and shift terrestrial compute burdens into space by **2030**.
* **Tony Kim:** AGI for classical computing will emerge around **2028 to 2030**.
* **Tony Kim:** Foundation labs will go public within the next **12 months**.

## Notable Quotes
> "The base layer of compute went up 10,000x—a $10,000 server is a million-dollar server... I don't think people realize that we are that compute-hardware-centric now. Before AI, in the BCE era, it was probably reversed."
> — Tony Kim

> "The irony of it all is that the trillion dollars of CapEx this year and the $10 trillion over the next five years that are coming is to move data centimeters and millimeters. That's AI."
> — Tony Kim

> "It's not a revenge of the nerds. It's the lost ring of power that was found... Chips were never a commodity; they have the highest profitability of any company or sector in the world."
> — Tony Kim

briefings.title: Build Hour: Valuemaxxing with GPT-5.6
briefings.tldr: OpenAI introduced the GPT-5.6 family (Sol, Terra, and Luna) and shifted the developer focus from "token-maxing" (measuring progress by AI volume) to "value-maxxing" (measuring outcomes and cost-performance).
briefings.summary_markdown:
## TL;DR
OpenAI introduced the GPT-5.6 family (Sol, Terra, and Luna) and shifted the developer focus from "token-maxing" (measuring progress by AI volume) to "value-maxxing" (measuring outcomes and cost-performance). Ploy shared how they migrated their production marketing agent to GPT-5.6, achieving a 2.2× faster build speed at a 27% lower cost through rigorous prompt caching, tool optimization, and breakpoint management.

## 1. Shift from Token-Maxing to Value-Maxxing
* **The Token-Maxing Trap:** 
  * Defined by measuring progress through raw AI volume (tokens burned, prompts sent, concurrent agents managed).
  * Led to companies burning through annual AI budgets in months and enterprises throttling spend.
* **The Value-Maxxing Philosophy:**
  * **Core Definition:** Measuring progress by what AI accomplishes—outcomes, time saved, and artifact quality.
  * **Strategic Spending:** Spending more tokens is justified if it drives proportional value (e.g., higher reasoning levels for quality, faster time-to-completion for migrations, scaling proven workflows, or using LLMs-as-a-judge for risk management).

## 2. GPT-5.6 Model Family & Codex Best Practices (Charlie Guo - DevEx, OpenAI)
* **Model Tiering:**
  * **Sol:** Flagship frontier model for complex coding and professional tasks.
  * **Terra:** Balanced daily driver for workloads balancing intelligence, cost, and latency.
  * **Luna:** High-volume workloads prioritizing low cost and fast latency over deep intelligence.
* **Codex Optimization Tips:**
  * **Reasoning Level Rule of Thumb:** Start with **Sol on Medium** rather than defaulting to extra-high/Max for routine day-to-day work.
  * **Speed vs. Tokens:** Turn on **Fast mode** to run outputs at 1.5x speed (consuming limits faster to save human time).
  * **Permissions & Memory:** Use **auto-approval** (avoiding full-access security risks while bypassing per-action permission fatigue) and **Chronicle** (screen recording memory for repeating tasks).
  * **Prompt Dieting:** Audit `AGENTS.md` and skill instructions to remove outdated, verbose constraints and save input tokens.

## 3. API Harness Features for Cost-Performance (Charlie Guo & Team)
* **Programmatic Tool Calling:**
  * Gives the model a JavaScript sandbox to write and execute code, call tools, and run computations.
  * **Savings:** Removes math/logic from the model's chain of thought, saving **24% fewer input tokens** and cutting an entire model round-trip.
* **Prompt Caching & Persistence:**
  * **Placement Strategy:** Append dynamic variables (like the current date) to the *end* of prompts so the large static prefix remains cacheable.
  * **Results:** Caching static system prompts and large context cuts input costs by **90%**.
  * **Persistent Reasoning:** Preserves reasoning terms across turns, boosting capability and cache efficiency.
* **Context Compaction:**
  * Triggering auto-compaction on long conversation histories yielded **82% fewer input tokens** (dropping from 24,000 to just over 4,000 tokens on a test query).

## 4. Real-World Migration: Ploy's Production Agent Case Study (Bryant Chou & Lorenzo Gentile - Ploy)
* **Company Background:**
  * Founded by Bryant Chou (co-founder and CTO of Webflow for 12.5 years; YC batch alum with 13% of the latest batch using Ploy).
  * Ploy converts existing websites into bespoke design systems within 60 seconds and runs autonomous marketing funnels (SEO, de-anonymization, lead qualification, and CRM sync).
* **Caching & Breakpoint Architecture (Lorenzo Gentile):**
  * **The KV Cache Challenge:** Standard agent loops create $N^2$ token processing growth as context accumulates; modifying tools or system prompts breaks the cache.
  * **On-Demand Tools:** Core tools (used in >70% of sessions) are always on; niche tools are loaded on-demand by appending schemas to the *end* of the context window to preserve the cache. Result: **45% reduction** in tool schema tokens and **33% cost reduction**.
  * **Breakpoint Caching:** Placing cache breakpoints after static system prompts/tools and after workspace memory yields an **89% reduction** in first-message tokens for new chats and a **5% overall production token reduction**.
* **Tool Batching & Slimming:**
  * **Batching Actions:** Prompting agents to combine independent tool calls into a single step (or designing tools to perform multiple actions, like reading two files at once) cuts out redundant context re-processing, saving **14% on costs**.
  * **Search Optimization:** Switching the web search provider (Exa) to use "Highlights" slimmed down tool response sizes by **70%**, generating an estimated **$37,000/year in token savings** without quality loss on evals.
  * **Deterministic vs. Agentic:** Offloading deterministic logic entirely away from the agent loop reduced token spend by **54%**.

## 5. Q&A Insights: Reasoning Modes, Sub-Agents, & Chat Management
* **Reasoning Modes (Max & Ultra):**
  * **Max:** Fully removes the leash on reasoning effort above extra-high.
  * **Pro:** Available via API parameters (`reasoning mode: Pro`) for ChatGPT-level reasoning depth (spending significantly more tokens and latency).
  * **Ultra:** A mode built on top of Max reasoning that modifies the system prompt to natively dispatch sub-agents (ideal for heavy workloads, but "brings a bazooka to a knife fight" for simple tasks).
* **Sub-Agent Context & Depth:**
  * Sub-agents are typically given specific context required for their delegated task by the orchestrator rather than a full forked context window.
  * Going past two layers of sub-agent depth risks losing context; wider, shallower agent structures with parallelized lanes are generally more effective unless using frontier orchestration models like GPT-5.6 Sol.
* **Chat Management:** While compaction handles long threads well, starting a new chat remains useful when a project's default setup is heavily loaded with plugins, skills, or attachments.

## 6. Notable Quotes
> *"Value-maxxing in contrast with token-maxxing... is measuring progress not by how much AI you are using, but what AI is actually helping you to accomplish, how much work you're getting done, how much time are you saving."* — Charlie Guo

> *"Every byte a tool returns becomes future input. Return the minimum evidence needed for the next decision. Make deterministic work deterministic."* — Lorenzo Gentile

> *"As a startup, we're constantly looking for some type of alpha... you really just have to try every single model that's out there... and stress test whether or not they fit Ploy's use cases."* — Bryant Chou

briefings.title: GTC SJ 2026: Next Generation Intelligent Surgical Robots
briefings.tldr: Next-generation surgical robots are shifting toward data-centric, Ethernet-based architectures that use AI foundational models, real-time edge compute, and agentic workflows to improve surgical efficiency and enable advanced autonomy.
briefings.summary_markdown:
## TL;DR
Next-generation surgical robots are shifting toward data-centric, Ethernet-based architectures that use AI foundational models, real-time edge compute, and agentic workflows to improve surgical efficiency and enable advanced autonomy.

## State-of-the-Art vs. Data-Centric Architectures
* **Current Surgical Robotic Limitations:** 
  * Today's systems rely heavily on Level 1 autonomy (teleoperated robots) and closed, proprietary cabling/protocols between components.
  * Distributed setups create massive complexity and maintenance overhead when moving between product generations.
* **The Data-Centric Shift:** 
  * Modeled after autonomous vehicles and next-gen humanoids, future robots use a centralized data-center-on-wheels approach over unified Ethernet.
  * **Unified I/O & RDMA:** The **Holoscan sensor bridge** (free and open-source FPGA IP) converts signals (CSI MIPI, SPI, I2C, GPIO) to Ethernet, enabling Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) straight to GPU memory.
  * **Low-Latency Performance:** Achieves speed-of-light implementations down to **1.2ms** from sensor input to output controller (compared to ~50ms in legacy systems).

## Edge Computing and Compute Requirements
* **IGX Thor Platform:** High-end edge compute (**IGX Thor T7000**) delivers over **5,000 Teraflops of FP4** for inference, 128GB of memory, and **400 Gbps** of Ethernet bandwidth (double the previous generation's 700 Gbps, with 800 Gbps targeted next).
* **3-Computer Solution Workflow:** Integrates training, simulation, and deployment into a continuous flywheel that uses the same software brain in both digital twins and physical systems.

## Datasets and Next-Generation AI Models
* **Open-H Embodiment Coalition:** 
  * Built with luminary partners (including Axel Krieger at JHU and Nasir Navab at TUM), growing from 3 to **35 partner organizations** across industry, academia, and healthcare.
  * Features 8 robotic embodiments spanning simulation, table-top, ex-vivo, animal, and clinical data (e.g., **CMR Surgical** donated nearly **500 hours** of kinematics and video data).
  * Hosted on Hugging Face as a **4-terabyte dataset**, achieving over **1,000 downloads** in its first few days.
* **Vision-Language-Action (VLA) Models:** 
  * *Classical VLAs:* Built on Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and fine-tuned on task data (e.g., JHU's SutureBot) to perform end-to-end tasks like suturing.
  * *World Foundation Model VLAs:* Newer architectures use generative World Foundation Models (like those from **Semaphor Surgical**) for kinematics and video generation, outperforming classical VLAs.
* **Cosmos-H Surgical Simulator:** 
  * Open-sourced model driven by robot kinematics and ground-truth frames to simulate 8 different embodiments.
  * Runs at **12 frames per second** on a single **RTX Pro 6000 GPU** (with real-time distillation underway).
* **Real-Time Telesurgery Tokenizers:** Neural tokenizers encode surgical video into latent space, rivaling traditional JPEG compression quality.

## Smart Hospitals and Agentic Systems
* **Operating Room Economics & Pressures:** 
  * OR time costs **$46 per minute** in the US across over **50,000 ORs**.
  * Surgical suites generate **60% or more** of hospital revenue.
  * The global healthcare workforce faces a **15 million worker shortage by 2030**, while global surgical volume is projected to **rise by 50% over the next 9 years**.
* **Rheo Workflow & Physical Agents:** 
  * Published as part of Isaac for Healthcare 0.5, using digital twins and generative AI (Cosmos Transfer) for synthetic data generation.
  * Demonstrated via **Peritus robots** that monitor OR workflow phases, verify tray inventory via room cameras, and autonomously fetch missing surgical trays from the Sterile Processing Department (SPD).

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* *Real-Time World Foundation Models:* Real-time operation of World Foundation Models for robotic interaction will be achieved **within the next 6 months** — Sean Hoover.
* *Telesurgery Latency Moonshot:* An experimental setup combining neural tokenizers and World Foundation Models to actively shave network latency in telesurgery will launch **later this year** — Sean Hoover.

## Notable Quotes
> *"If you are a researcher, if you are a PhD student and you happen to be at a university that does not have a DVRK, you're kind of out of luck. There's only three and a half hours of open-source data... put out by Johns Hopkins called the JIGSAWS dataset."*
> — **Sean Hoover**

> *"Every minute in the operating room in US costs around $46 in US, and there are over 50,000 operating rooms, just do the math. Surgical suites represent, 60% or more of the hospital revenue and there's shortage of 15 million healthcare workers globally by 2030."*
> — **Mahdi Azizian**

briefings.title: Google's Negative Cash Flow and the AI Capex Reckoning | The Weekly Wrap
briefings.tldr: Google and Tesla saw their shares drop significantly after posting negative free cash flow driven by surging AI capital expenditure, signaling a major shift in investor sentiment toward the capital intensity of the AI trade.
briefings.summary_markdown:
## TL;DR
Google and Tesla saw their shares drop significantly after posting negative free cash flow driven by surging AI capital expenditure, signaling a major shift in investor sentiment toward the capital intensity of the AI trade.

## Geopolitical Tensions & Broad Market Indicators
- **Iran War & Oil Prices:** US and Iran traded blows over the weekend with reported US soldier casualties; the Houthis subsequently bombed Saudi tankers.
    - **Market Impact:** Oil prices climbed to $100 and the 10-year yield reached 4.7%; President Trump threatened additional attacks on Iran.
- **SpaceX:** Trading well below its IPO price, signaling potential headwinds for the broader IPO market.
- **K-Shaped Economy (Domino's Pizza):** Stock is down 20% this year. Q2 EPS was up 7% (missing expectations) on a revenue beat that drove a 2% stock bump on Monday, but same-store sales growth fell to a 5-quarter low of 0.1% before the stock gave up all gains and more.

## Corporate Earnings & Sector Performance
- **Equifax (Credit Bureau / SAS-pocalypse Debate):** 
    - **Business Mix:** Heavily mortgage-dependent on scoring, but its largest division is Workforce Solutions (EWS), a B2B/government automated income and employment verification software business.
    - **Q2 Results:** Government revenue growth fell mid--single digits (missing management's flat guidance and street expectations). Q3 EPS guidance is 3% below consensus, and implied Q4 EPS guidance is also 3% below street estimates (blamed on state government budget concerns).
    - **Stock Impact:** Down 17% YTD and 30% over the last year prior to the report; dropped an additional 4% on the news.
- **General Motors (Automotive):** 
    - **Results:** Reported EPS of $3.57 vs. $2.53 last year (41% growth) and a big beat over expectations of $3.19; raised full-year profit guidance and stock was up.
    - **Caveat:** Despite raised guidance, US sales fell year-over-year, including large pickup trucks and SUVs which drive most of GM's earnings.
- **Northrop Grumman & Lockheed Martin (Defense):**
    - **Northrop Grumman:** EPS of $7.68 vs. $8.15 last year and $6.82 expected with a revenue beat. Backlog increased by $20 billion to a record $105 billion, and EPS guidance was raised. However, open-ended cost growth on missile programs hurt current margins and weighed on the stock open.
    - **Lockheed Martin:** Posted strong Q2 2026 results with sales up 11% and EPS of $7.94 vs. $1.46 last year and $7.20 expected, plus a revenue beat. Backlog reached a record $230 billion (up 24% in three months).
- **GE Vernova (AI Power Infrastructure):**
    - **Business:** Produces large gas turbines (alongside Mitsubishi and Siemens) and utility electrification equipment. Spun out of GE in April 2024 at $143, climbing over $1,000 as a premier AI power play.
    - **Results:** EPS of $2.47 (33% growth, but a miss); revenue of $11.1 billion (up 22% YoY); orders of $24.2 billion (up 88% YoY), lifting backlog to $176 billion. Raised revenue and EPS guidance, though the raise fell below whisper numbers, causing the stock to drop.
- **Moody's (Credit Ratings Duopoly):**
    - **Results:** EPS of $4.68 (up 31% YoY). Stock has been flat since fall 2024, bringing the 2026 PE multiple down to sub-30x (its cheapest in quite some time) amid unfounded AI disruption fears.
- **Google (AI Capex & Free Cash Flow):**
    - **Results:** Adjusted EPS of $2.85 vs. $2.31 last year (missing expectations of $2.89, excluding massive investment gains). Revenue grew 24%, with Google Cloud revenue reaching $24.8 billion (up 82%).
    - **The Negative:** Massive AI capex pushed free cash flow into negative territory at -$5.9 billion. Google upped its 2026 AI capex spend from $190 billion to $205 billion. Stock fell 7% after hours.
- **Tesla (EVs & Capex):**
    - **Results:** EPS of $0.33 vs. $0.40 last year and $0.51 expected (a big miss). Revenue was solid at $28 billion vs. $26 billion expected.
    - **The Negative:** Margins under pressure due to a 67% decline in regulatory credits (eliminated by the Trump administration) and a capex increase to $5.8 billion. Free cash flow turned negative for the first time in two years at -$1.1 billion. Stock fell 14.5% after hours.
- **IBM (Hardware & Mainframes):**
    - **Results:** In line with its prior negative pre-announcement. EPS of $2.93 (up 5% YoY). Cut revenue growth forecast to 4-5%. Data center mainframe sales dropped 42% and infrastructure revenue fell 7% YoY as tech equipment prices soar and clients lock in purchases over services.
- **ServiceNow (Software / SAS-pocalypse):**
    - **Results:** EPS of $0.90 (up 10% YoY); revenue reached $4 billion (up 24% YoY). Stock down 38% YTD due to the software AI narrative despite showing zero operational weakness; dropped another ~4% on the earnings print.
- **Blackstone (Private Equity):**
    - **Results:** EPS of $1.52 vs. $1.21 last year and $1.36 expected, driven by higher transaction revenues and strong performance fees from better realizations. Fundraising was strong at $68 billion.
    - **Headwinds:** Slow base management fee growth, modestly positive performance in real estate and credit, lengthening asset realization times, and private credit software refinancing risks looming next year. Management noted it is the biggest financier of AI data centers.
- **Intel (Semiconductors):**
    - **Results:** EPS of $42 cents vs. a loss of $10 cents last year. Revenue growth was the best in 15 years, with data center segment sales soaring 59% YoY. Stock was up after hours.

## The Shift in the AI Narrative
- **Capital Intensity:** The market is losing patience with ever-mounting AI capex budgets (exemplified by Google raising spend to $205 billion and posting negative FCF).
- **Lack of Moats & Price Wars:** Chinese AI player Moonshot announced the release of its new LLM model, Kimi K3, which matches top LLMs at a fraction of the cost, raising fears of an impending price war.
- **Market Reaction:** Discontent with negative cash flows at Google (-7%) and Tesla (-14.5%) dragged the Nasdaq down over 2% on Thursday.

## Mailbag: Banks & Shorting Mechanics
- **Bank Stocks & Tech Correlation (Pedro):**
    - **Bank of New York (BNY):** A trust bank operating in its own league alongside State Street; up over 30% this year, matching general large-cap bank performance.
    - **Eisman's Bank Holdings:** Owns zero banks (last owned Citigroup before CEO Jane Fraser, selling after trading scandals). Prefers tech research.
    - **Hesitation:** Banks are at peak valuations after a strong run, and current investment banking cycles are heavily tied to AI financing needs—meaning buying major banks (Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs, Bank of America, Citigroup) offers zero diversification away from tech exposure.
- **Funding Shorts Explained (Colin):**
    - **Standard Short:** Borrow a stock, sell it at $100 for cash, buy it back later at $50, return it to the owner, and pocket the $50 spread (minus borrow fees).
    - **Funding Short:** Borrow a stock and sell it at $100 to generate $100 in cash, then immediately use that cash to buy stock in a high-conviction long position. The goal is to make substantial gains on the long while breaking even or making a small return on the short position.

briefings.title: How Photoroom Trained Themselves To Dream Bigger
briefings.tldr: Mathieu Rouif and Eliot Andres share how going through Y Combinator transformed Photoroom from a vague dream into a massive global company, providing the playbooks, mindset shifts, and tactical frameworks needed for European founders to scale their ambition.
briefings.summary_markdown:
## TL;DR
Mathieu Rouif and Eliot Andres share how going through Y Combinator transformed Photoroom from a vague dream into a massive global company, providing the playbooks, mindset shifts, and tactical frameworks needed for European founders to scale their ambition.

---

## Photoroom Scale and Background
- **Core Product:** AI visuals that help e-commerce businesses grow and sell.
- **Current Scale:** 300 million downloads, 20 million active users.
- **Enterprise Adoption:** Used by major global e-commerce companies including Amazon, Uber, DoorDash, and Decathlon.
- **Batch Milestone:** Recognized by Gary Tan as the largest YC company with a headquarters in Europe.

---

## The YC Ambition Shift: From Dream to Playbook
- **Concrete Playbooks:** Before YC, building a $1 billion company felt like a distant, non-concrete dream. Interacting with peers and partners who had built $10 billion companies made the scale feel tangible and achievable.
- **Demo Day Results:** Photoroom went from 0 to $1M during their remote batch, finishing as the fastest-growing company of the batch, which proved the math worked in their favor.
- **Continuous Benchmarking:** Even post-batch, YC retreats and ongoing partner meetings expose founders to extreme scale—such as 19-year-olds launching satellites into space—resetting the benchmark for what is possible.

---

## Overcoming European Cultural Barriers to Ambition
- **Cultural Skepticism:** In Europe, pitching a big idea often invites laughter or criticism, whereas the default reaction in the US is encouragement.
- **Failure Tolerance:** Unlike ecosystems where failure is valued as a learning experience that makes a candidate more hirable, European cultures often attach a social penalty to failure.
- **The Talent Confidence Gap:** 
  - **French Engineer Example:** Offered a role, declined out of fear that the team was too strong and they would fail.
  - **American Engineer Example:** Overconfident, accepted the offer, and successfully negotiated for compensation two levels above the baseline.

---

## Tactical Frameworks for Aiming Higher
- **The Magic Wand Exercise:** List current options and career levels, then use a thought exercise to determine the level just above, the level 10X above, and the level of a universe king with zero constraints.
- **Add a Zero:** Implement Sam Altman’s advice to add a zero to any success metric or target to force creative problem-solving around how to reach it.
- **Global Mindset Filtering:** Enforce English as the primary internal language (even between French co-founders) in the Paris office as a deliberate filter to hire talent committed to building a global company.
- **Depth as Ambition:** Focus aggressively to compound growth—Photoroom grew 10X by narrowing from video/photo to photo, and another 10X by focusing specifically on e-commerce photo.
- **V-Zero Prototyping:** Cut project scopes down to the bare minimum (v-zero) to test and learn in days rather than spending three months building the wrong thing.

---

## Predictions & Forward Calls
*There are no genuine forward-looking claims, concrete timelines, or future predictions stated in this transcript.*

---

## Notable Quotes
> "If you look at the curve of the times at marathons, there's a spike at 2:30 and 3 hours because people say, 'Oh, I'm going to do it in three hours,' and they force themselves and so it's the same with targets. You can just say, 'Okay, here's the goal,' and then you walk back from there."
> — **Mathieu Rouif**

> "Shoot for the stars, worst case you land on the moon."
> — **Nico** (Quoted by Matt)

> "Don't misinterpret like depth with ambition. So being deep is actually a great way to achieve ambition."
> — **Mathieu Rouif**

briefings.title: How Two French Engineers In New York Built The Company That Monitors The Entire Cloud
briefings.tldr: Datadog CEO Olivier Pomel reflects on building a multi-product cloud monitoring giant from New York, emphasizing the power of bottom-up adoption, obsessive customer feedback loops, and the urgent necessity of moving faster on hiring and firing.
briefings.summary_markdown:
## TL;DR
Datadog CEO Olivier Pomel reflects on building a multi-product cloud monitoring giant from New York, emphasizing the power of bottom-up adoption, obsessive customer feedback loops, and the urgent necessity of moving faster on hiring and firing.

## Background & Origin Story
- **Roots in New York:** Graduated from Centrale in 1999, did an internship at IBM Research in upstate New York, and stayed through the dot-com boom, bust, and September 11th.
- **The Educational Software Precursor:** Worked with co-founder Alexis at an educational software startup that grew to roughly 800 people, where Olivier led dev and Alexis led tech ops.
- **The DevOps Insight:** Experienced firsthand the friction between developers and operations teams; realized bringing DevOps together into one platform was the missing puzzle piece.
- **The YC Rejection:** Applied to Y Combinator and was rejected by Paul Graham (received a rejection email, and later an accidental invite retraction); framed the rejection email as motivation.
- **Painful Early Fundraising:** Angel round was super painful; New York VCs didn't understand the competitive landscape, and Valley VCs thought it was a "form of mental impairment" to start an infrastructure company outside the Bay Area.

## Product Strategy & Cloud Tailwinds
- **Riding the Cloud Explosion:** Started in 2010 when companies dismissed AWS as a "toy"; targeting small, modern, cloud-first companies proved to be the ultimate tailwind.
- **Category Naming:** Shifted initial descriptions from a vague "data platform for DevOps collaboration" to **Infrastructure Monitoring**, which immediately resonated with buyers and bosses.
- **Portfolio Expansion:** Grew to **20–25 products**, driven by observing customer extensions, internal workflows, and forward-looking "strategic" bets.
- **The AI Shift:** The company serves the top 10 AI companies in the world alongside traditional enterprises (banks, train companies); building observability for agents and baking intelligence directly into the data plane.

## Culture, Leadership, and Staying Grounded
- **No Written Culture Document:** Refuses to put core values on the wall, believing culture flows directly from the top through everyday actions, hiring, and firing.
- **Reading Raw Feedback:** Continually samples actual support requests, sales transcripts, customer feedback, and employee survey comments rather than relying on polished executive summaries.
- **Challenging the Chain of Command:** Randomly drops questions into Slack or email threads regarding low-level complaints, forcing management to stay dialed into ground-level realities.
- **Public Markets Reality:** Went public on March 2019; the lock-up expiration coincided with the COVID lockdown day market crash, causing the stock to drop roughly 65% (from a $10B valuation down to ~$4B) before rebounding.

## AI Impact & Engineering Transformation
- **No-Code Directive:** Co-founder Alexis told the engineering team that within **two quarters**, they won't be writing code anymore.
- **Hack Project Evidence:** Over the holidays in December, excellent developers independently rebuilt whole systems in a couple of days that would have previously required a team of six over six months.
- **Organizational Agility:** Shifted the organization to take more shots, move faster, and accept being wrong more often because smaller teams can now explore ideas previously requiring massive headcount.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
- **AI-Driven Code Generation:** "In two quarters, we're not writing any, any code anymore" — Olivier Pomel (citing his co-founder's directive on the inversion of software development).

## Notable Quotes
> "Culture flows from the top. So we exemplify the culture, we hire, we promote, we fire based on the culture, and to date, that still works."
> — Olivier Pomel

> "Your job is not to understand what I want, as a boss, your job is to understand what's happening within your span of control, and listen to it very, very precisely."
> — Olivier Pomel

> "The one lesson I keep learning all the time, so, is that you should always move faster, especially when it comes to hiring and firing."
> — Olivier Pomel

briefings.title: 'Inference Speed Makes Markets Bigger,' says Cerebras CEO
briefings.tldr: Cerebras Systems and AMD are partnering on a joint server architecture that combines AMD’s Helios GPUs (to process prompts) with Cerebras servers (to generate answers at high speeds) to create an ultra-fast inference pipeline.
briefings.summary_markdown:
**TL;DR:** Cerebras Systems and AMD are partnering on a joint server architecture that combines AMD’s Helios GPUs (to process prompts) with Cerebras servers (to generate answers at high speeds) to create an ultra-fast inference pipeline. Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman emphasizes that speed expands the entire AI market by increasing productivity.

## The AMD-Cerebras Partnership & Server Architecture
* **Two-Part Inference Workflow:** 
  * **Prompt Processing:** Handled by AMD's Helios systems, which excel at parallelizing the analysis of queries.
  * **Answer Generation:** Handled by Cerebras servers, which generate responses at extraordinary speeds.
* **Open Standards Approach:** 
  * Unlike proprietary walled gardens, Cerebras utilizes open standards-based technology for its I/O.
  * This open approach has enabled quick integrations with multiple chipmakers, including AMD and AWS (with Trainium).
* **Historical Ties & Equity:** 
  * Feldman has known AMD CEO Lisa Su for decades, dating back to when AMD acquired his previous company.
  * AMD has been an equity investor in Cerebras for quite some time, participating in mid and later-stage funding rounds.

## Market Strategy & Economics
* **Market Expansion:** 
  * **Speed Makes Markets Bigger:** Feldman argues that fast inference is productive inference, and when AI is productive, people are willing to spend more rather than fight over a fixed-size market.
* **Avoiding HBM Constraints:** 
  * Cerebras does not use High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), allowing them to generate tokens at a lower cost without depending on supply-chain-constrained parts.

## Global AI Landscape & Cost Dynamics
* **US vs. China Approaches:** 
  * Addressing comments from SK Group Chair Chey Tae-won regarding China's focus on the lowest dollar-per-token versus America's focus on quality non-HBM tokens, Feldman notes it remains an open question whether Chinese model makers achieve lower costs through genuine invention or by distilling and piggybacking on US technology.
* **Open Weight Debate:** 
  * Regarding tech leaders emphasizing US focus on open weights, Feldman notes that OpenAI and Anthropic created the market through massive investments, while followers use fast-follow strategies. Cerebras focuses strictly on driving up productivity by delivering more tokens faster per unit of power and dollar.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **Deployment Timeline:** The first application of the joint AMD-Cerebras solution will launch in the Cerebras Cloud later this year, followed shortly by general availability — Andrew Feldman

## Notable Quotes
> *"Speed makes markets bigger, right? It doesn't make markets smaller. This isn't about carving up something that's of fixed size... Fast, fast inference is productive inference. And where AI is productive, people are willing to spend more and more and more."* — **Andrew Feldman**

> *"By being open, by being standards based, half the leading chip makers, AMD, AWS with Trainium are now using our solution in a disaggregated approach for high speed inference delivery."* — **Andrew Feldman**

briefings.title: Opencode CEO: Blocked, 20X Growth in 6 Months, Building the Coding Agent for the World
briefings.tldr: Opencode, an open-source coding agent that works with any model, scaled to 13 million monthly active users and 7 trillion daily tokens processed, driven by a 16-year overnight success story of persistence.
briefings.summary_markdown:
## TL;DR
Opencode, an open-source coding agent that works with any model, scaled to 13 million monthly active users and 7 trillion daily tokens processed, driven by a 16-year overnight success story of persistence.

## Scale and Explosive Growth
- **User and Token Volume:**
  - Reached **4.6 million weekly active users** and **13 million monthly active users** by the end of June, representing a **20X increase** since the beginning of the year.
  - Processes approximately **7 trillion tokens per day** (surpassing OpenRouter's 6 trillion daily tokens).
- **Revenue Run Rate:**
  - Inference business annualized run rate sits between **$38M to nearly $40M** (extrapolated from recent weekly data), built in about 8 months since launching in late September/early October.
  - Subscription plan (**"OpenCode Go"** at $10/month), launched in late February/early March, grew to **160,000 monthly subscribers** generating about **$18 million** in annualized revenue.
- **Ecosystem Adoption:**
  - **Codex Integration:** Codex officially supports OpenCode; roughly **5% of all Codex subscribers** choose OpenCode as their main harness to use underlying APIs.
  - **Enterprise Footprint:** Dozens of top Fortune 500 companies have thousands of employees using OpenCode internally, prompting inbounds for enterprise security questionnaires.

## The Anthropic Controversy & Global Distribution
- **The Anthropic Catalyst:**
  - In the first week of January, when monthly users were at **650,000**, Anthropic attempted to block Claude Code subscriptions from being used within OpenCode by rejecting system prompts containing the word "OpenCode."
  - This enforcement inadvertently put OpenCode and Claude Code on the same pedestal, equating the two products and driving massive brand awareness and new user acquisition.
- **Global User Demographics:**
  - **China:** Accounts for **17%** of traffic on the OpenCode Go plan (making Opencode a rare YC company with meaningful usage in China, driven by domestic preference for local models like GLM).
  - **Developing Markets:** Highly popular in price-sensitive regions where a $200/month subscription is prohibitive, including **Brazil (5%)**, **Indonesia (4%)**, and **Vietnam**.
  - **United States:** Experiencing strong growth despite initial expectations that US users would stick exclusively to premium frontier subscriptions.

## Model Dynamics & Open Source Economics
- **Model Shift:** 
  - Open-source models crossed a viability threshold for real work in February, notably when models like Kimmy (e.g., Kimmy 2.5) briefly flipped usage metrics to surpass Anthropic models over a 4-week span among OpenCode users.
- **Token Usage Breakdown:**
  - **DeepSeek Flash** is heavily utilized as a cost-effective fallback when users approach daily or weekly limits.
  - **GLM (e.g., GLM 5.2)** drives heavy usage due to perceived superiority in front-end design.
- **GPU Inference Stability:** 
  - Because of global usage across the East and West work cycles, Opencode maintains a remarkably stable 24-hour GPU utilization cycle, creating a structural unit-economics advantage over region-specific competitors.

## Product Architecture & Strategic Intent
- **Core Architecture:** 
  - Opencode operates as a two-part product: a terminal UI application and an agent server loop (which companies like Ramp previously embedded behind custom Slack bots).
- **Deliberate Positioning:**
  - **Naming Strategy:** The name "OpenCode" was a deliberate choice to capture the open alternative position when dominant players control the market, following a similar playbook to their past project "OpenNext."
  - **Dataset Creation:** Built `models.dev`, an open-source dataset tracking over 70 models and providers, to establish default status in multi-model routing.
  - **Terminal-First UX:** Designed by NeoVim/Vim users to feel like a modern, high-performance terminal experience, differentiating itself from IDE-heavy tools like Cursor.

## 16-Year Origin Story
- **Founding Timeline:**
  - CEO J.V. started the company with college roommate Frank in **2006/2007** as sophomores at the University of Waterloo, incorporating the legal entity in **2010** (a **16-year-old legal entity**).
  - Applied to Y Combinator **nine times** between 2016 and 2021, enduring four interviews before finally getting accepted into the **2021 batch** with a serverless framework project (which eventually tied into OpenCode).
- **Team Continuity:**
  - J.V. and Frank operated as a two-person co-founder team for over a decade before adding a third co-founder four years ago.
- **Building in Public:**
  - Shifted to public metrics and open development around 2022 following encouragement from Dalton and co-founder Dax, turning their journey into a public-facing reality show for the developer community.

## Notable Quotes
> "You really know you have product market fit when like, enterprises are bugging you to sign the security agreements so they can use your product. It's like, please do this, because I, I don't know who you guys are, but a bunch of us are using this."
> — J.V.

> "When you've got a dominant or, in this case, two dominant players in the market, the rest of the market coalesces around an open alternative and picking that position ends up being really valuable because if you pick it, it's very hard for somebody else to displace you."
> — J.V.

> "To catch lightning in the bottle, you actually like have to sort of position the bottle correctly and be ready for it and know what to do with it."
> — Harj Taggar

briefings.title: The Fight Over Open Source AI, Anthropic's $1.5B Payout, NYC Socialists: Evictions = Violence?
briefings.tldr: The All-In podcasters debate the escalating threats to the open source AI ecosystem amid panic over Chinese model releases, analyze Anthropic's historic $1.5 billion copyright settlement, and critique progressive housing policies in New York City as a dangerous erosion of private property rights.
briefings.summary_markdown:
## TL;DR
The All-In podcasters debate the escalating threats to the open source AI ecosystem amid panic over Chinese model releases, analyze Anthropic's historic $1.5 billion copyright settlement, and critique progressive housing policies in New York City as a dangerous erosion of private property rights.

## The Fight to Save Open Source AI & The China Panic
* **The Kimi K3 Catalyst:** 
  * China's Moonshot AI released Kimi K3, an open-source model matching top proprietary performance at roughly 50% lower cost.
  * The White House faced conflicting internal pressure: Axios reported considerations of a ban on Chinese open-source models, while Commerce Department officials opposed a ban and favored incentivizing US open-source development.
  * Polymarket odds for a US government open-source model ban in 2026 jumped to 45%.
* **Distillation Debate & Regulatory Capture:**
  * **David Sacks** argued that Anthropic is engaging in regulatory capture, noting they grew from $10 billion to over $70 billion in ARR this year, and that banning open-source developers punishes American builders for Anthropic's failure to stop distillation.
  * **Chamath Palihapitiya** explained distillation as using an AI's output to train another model, calling accusations a "red herring" and noting that if frontier labs genuinely wanted to stop industrial-scale scraping, they would implement strict KYC checks instead of lobbying for government protection.
  * **David Friedberg** drew parallels to historical software benchmarking (such as early Google querying Yahoo and Microsoft), asserting that looking at model *outputs* rather than stealing proprietary *weights* is standard and not copyright infringement.
* **The Economic Commodity Trap:**
  * Palihapitiya and Friedberg argued that foundational models are rapidly commoditizing, shifting long-term value capture to the infrastructure layer (cloud providers, chips, energy) and the application layer above.
  * Sacks countered that both open and closed source will thrive, pointing to accelerating revenues at OpenAI and Anthropic despite open-source competition.

## Anthropic's $1.5B Piracy Settlement & IP Hypocrisy
* **Historic Payout:** 
  * Anthropic settled its major AI copyright lawsuit for $1.5 billion over training Claude on 7 million pirated books (covering 500,000 books thus far). 
  * Plaintiffs' lawyers took $101 million, while participating authors receive $3,000 per book (with a 91% claim rate among covered authors).
* **The IP Double Standard:** 
  * The hosts highlighted the hypocrisy of closed frontier labs defending their right to scrape the entire web under fair use (e.g., OpenAI's defense against the New York Times lawsuit) while condemning foreign or open-source competitors for utilizing public outputs.

## Market Shifts & Infrastructure Realities
* **Tech Capex & Cloud Demands:** 
  * Recent earnings from Google and Tesla highlighted the massive capital expenditures required to scale AI infrastructure.
  * Friedberg emphasized the extreme engineering hurdles of building cloud reliability, noting that moving from 99% uptime to "five nines" (99.999%) scales costs from millions to hundreds of billions of dollars.
* **Capital Allocation Critique:** 
  * Jason Calacanis criticized Apple's historical capital allocation, noting they spent $900 billion over the last decade ($755 billion in buybacks and $140 billion in dividends) rather than aggressively investing in transformative acquisitions or R&D.

## Socialism Corner: "Evictions = Violence" and Property Rights
* **New York City Housing Policies:** 
  * The podcasters discussed New York City Mayor/activist Zo Ram Mamdani introducing a rental reform package that freezes rents, bans credit/background checks and income standards (like the 40X rule) simultaneously, and legally recognizes tenant unions.
  * A clip from a hearing featured an activist referring to evictions as "the violence of evictions."
* **Economic Consequences of Anti-Landlord Policies:**
  * **David Friedberg** cited John Quincy Adams (1787/1791) to frame private property rights as the bedrock of American liberty, warning that socialist framing of landlords as "evil" is a slippery slope from anarchy to tyranny.
  * **David Sacks** noted that stripping landlords of the ability to evict unruly tenants or screen applicants turns apartment buildings into dilapidated housing projects, ultimately harming working-class neighbors and forcing landlords to keep units empty ("ghost apartments").
  * **Chamath Palihapitiya** pointed to empirical data from Austin, Texas, showing that relaxing permitting constraints and increasing housing supply naturally lowers rents, whereas price controls and eviction bans create market dysfunction.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **Chamath Palihapitiya:** Predicts that foundational AI models will commoditize within 5 to 7 to 10 years, shifting terminal value entirely to the application and infrastructure layers.
* **David Sacks:** Predicts that if the US government enacts a ban on open-source AI, it will "decapitate" the capital markets and force American enterprises to absorb a massive "token tax" compared to foreign competitors.
* **Polymarket/Markets:** Implied 45% probability that the US government will ban an open-source model in 2026.

## Notable Quotes
> "I think it would be a tragic mistake if the government were to take action against the open source ecosystem. That would do nothing but hurt America's position in this AI race." — **David Sacks**

> "This is a valuation preservation game by the closed frontier labs... In the absence of regulatory intervention, what will happen is that as people learn about how value is changing, they're going to put more value in the application layer and more value in the infrastructure layer." — **Chamath Palihapitiya**

> "The moment the idea is admitted into society that property is not as sacred as the laws of God... anarchy and tyranny commence. Property must be secured or liberty cannot exist." — **David Friedberg** (quoting John Quincy Adams)

briefings.title: The Invisible Backbone of AI: Why Light Powers Intelligence | Lumentum | RAISE Summit 2026
briefings.tldr: Michael Hurlston, CEO of Lumentum, and Tony Kim of BlackRock discuss how the exponential rise of AI model sizes is forcing data centers to transition from copper wiring to photonics (optics) across a four-stage framework: scale across, scale out, scale up, and scale in.
briefings.summary_markdown:
## TL;DR
Michael Hurlston, CEO of Lumentum, and Tony Kim of BlackRock discuss how the exponential rise of AI model sizes is forcing data centers to transition from copper wiring to photonics (optics) across a four-stage framework: scale across, scale out, scale up, and scale in.

## Data Center Evolution: From Copper to Optics
- **The Copper Wall:** As speeds and bandwidths increase inside data centers, the reach and capability of copper wiring decreases due to electrical resistance and heat.
- **The Physics Advantage of Light:** Optics eliminates resistance, allowing data to transmit over longer distances with far less loss compared to electrical signaling.
- **The Four-Stage Data Center Framework:**
  - **Scale Across (Kilometers):** The historic internet backbone connecting data centers; now operating at full bandwidth over kilometers to support massive inferencing models.
  - **Scale Out (Meters):** Connecting compute racks to switch banks using pluggable optical transceivers (roughly 10× the optical lanes of scale across).
  - **Scale Up (Inside the Rack / Centimeters to Meters):** Replacing internal rack copper links with optics to handle 1.6 terabits per second speeds; represents a 100× market expansion relative to scale across.
  - **Scale In (Millimeters / On-Chip & PCB):** Future transition to replace copper traces on printed circuit boards and disaggregate high-bandwidth memory from compute using optical interconnects (representing a 1,000× market scale).

## Optical Component Supply Chain & Manufacturing Challenges
- **Scale of Production Shift:** The optical industry historically served telecom customers (AT&T, Verizon) requiring hundreds of lasers; AI data centers now demand hundreds of millions of lasers.
- **Indium Phosphide Fab Constraints:** 
  - Lasers require a specialized light-emitting semiconductor material called **indium phosphide**.
  - Lumentum has brought online **5 different indium phosphide wafer fabs** to scale production from thousands of wafers to millions.
- **Industry Shortages:** Hurlston notes that severe supply shortages of indium phosphide will likely become even more acute than current memory chip shortages, prompting strategic investments from companies like NVIDIA into optical manufacturers.
- **Laser Density Requirements:** A typical Grace Blackwell server rack utilizing scale-up optics requires external pluggable light sources containing 8 distinct lasers each, totaling approximately **8,000 lasers per rack**.

## Laser Power Classes and Extreme Applications
- **Scale Out Power:** Modestly powered lasers operating at roughly **100 milliwatts**.
- **Scale Across and Scale Up Power:** Higher-powered lasers operating at roughly **400 milliwatts** to span kilometers or navigate rack-level distances.
- **Space and Undersea Deployments:** The same 400-milliwatt lasers used for scale-up and fiber optics (such as subsea cables in the Mariana Trench) can be adapted with amplification for free-space optics in satellite constellations and data centers in space.
- **Scale In Power:** Shorter-range, lower-power laser arrays designed to handle high data rates over millimeter and centimeter distances on printed circuit boards.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
- **Scale-Up Deployments:** First deployments of scale-up optics will occur in the **second half of 2027**, with optical racks appearing in mid-2027 and backplane connectivity following in **2028** — Michael Hurlston.
- **Scale-In Timeline:** Optical interconnects for on-chip and high-bandwidth memory disaggregation will begin to see adoption by the **end of the decade (2029)** — Michael Hurlston.

## Notable Quotes
> *"As speeds up, the reach of copper decreases... and copper isn't going to go away tomorrow, but as you're getting into these increasing speeds, these increasing bandwidths, what's ultimately happening is optics is necessary."*
> — **Michael Hurlston**

> *"This is an industry... that's used to telecom customers, AT&T, Verizon, and the numbers of lasers that those kind of customers would deploy are in the hundreds. Now we're talking about hundreds of millions."*
> — **Michael Hurlston**
